blocks.text: “You see, I do not know how to find any particular part of the diary.” As he spoke, an idea came to him. His voice changed. Without noticing it, he spoke simply and honestly, like a child: “That really is true. I give you my word. Honestly!” I could not help smiling, and he made a face. “I showed more about myself than I meant to that time!” he said. “But do you know something? I have kept the diary for months. Yet I never once thought about how to find a particular part if I wanted to look at it again.” By now I had decided something. This doctor had cared for Lucy. His diary might add to what we knew about that terrible Being. So I said boldly:—
“Then, Dr. Seward, you had better let me copy it out for you on my typewriter.” He became as pale as a dead man as he said:—
“No! no! no! Nothing in the world could make me let you know that terrible story!”

So it was terrible. My feeling had been right! I thought for a moment and looked around the room. Without knowing it, I was looking for something or some chance to help me. My eyes fell on a large pile of typed pages on the table. He noticed my look. Without thinking, he looked in the same direction. When he saw the pile, he understood what I meant.

“You do not know me,” I said. “You will know me better when you have read those papers. They are my own diary and my husband’s, which I have typed. To help with this work, I have shared every thought in my heart without holding back. But, of course, you do not know me—yet. I must not expect you to trust me so much.”

He is certainly a man with a good and generous heart. Poor dear Lucy was right about him. He stood up and opened a large drawer. Inside were several hollow metal tubes covered with dark wax, all arranged in order. He said:—

“You are quite right. I did not trust you because I did not know you. But I know you now. And let me say that I should have known you long ago. I know that Lucy told you about me. She told me about you too. May I do the only thing I can to make up for my mistake? Take the tubes and listen to them. The first six are about my personal life, and they will not fill you with horror. Then you will know me better. Dinner will be ready by then. While you listen, I shall read some of these papers. That will help me understand certain things better.” He himself carried the phonograph, the machine that plays recorded sounds, up to my sitting-room. He set it up for me. Now I am sure I shall learn something pleasant. It will tell me the other side of a true love story. I already know one side of it....

29 September.—I was so interested in Jonathan Harker’s wonderful diary and his wife’s diary that I forgot about time. Mrs. Harker had not come downstairs when the maid came to say dinner was ready. So I said: “Perhaps she is tired. Let dinner wait an hour.” Then I went on with my work. I had just finished Mrs. Harker’s diary when she came in. She looked sweet and pretty, but very sad. Her eyes were red from crying. Somehow this touched me deeply. God knows I have had reasons to cry lately! But I could not cry and feel the relief that tears bring. Now I saw those sweet eyes, still shining from her recent tears. The sight went straight to my heart. So I said as gently as I could:—
“I am very afraid that I have upset you.”

“Oh, no, you have not upset me,” she replied. “But your deep sadness has touched me more than I can say. That is a wonderful machine, but it tells the truth so exactly that it is cruel. The very sound of your voice told me of the terrible suffering in your heart. It was like a soul crying out to God, who has power over everything. No one must ever hear those words spoken again! See, I have tried to be useful. I have copied out the words on my typewriter. Now no one else needs to hear your heart beat as I did.”
